DECOLONIZATION — GLOBAL MAP AND TIMELINE
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  1947-1950: South Asia, Southeast Asia
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ India/Pakistan (1947), Burma, Ceylon (1948)             │
  │ Indonesia (1945/49), Philippines (1946)                 │
  │ Israel (1948) — end of British Mandate                  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  1951-1960: North Africa, West Africa
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Libya (1951), Sudan (1956), Morocco/Tunisia (1956)      │
  │ Ghana (1957) — first sub-Saharan African independence   │
  │ Guinea (1958), many French West/Equatorial Africa (1960)│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  1960s: "Year of Africa" (1960) + East/Central Africa
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 17 African states independent in 1960 alone             │
  │ Congo crisis (1960-65), Tanzania (1961), Uganda (1962)  │
  │ Algeria (1962) — after savage war                       │
  │ Aden/Yemen (1967), Zambia (1964), Malawi (1964)         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  1970s: Southern Africa and remaining holdouts
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Portuguese colonies (1974-75): Angola, Mozambique,      │
  │ Guinea-Bissau — after Carnation Revolution in Portugal  │
  │ Zimbabwe/Rhodesia (1980) — settler resistance           │
  │ Djibouti (1977), Suriname (1975)                        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PERSISTENCE: Western Sahara (disputed), Falklands (British)
               Hong Kong returned 1997, Macau 1999

WHO DROVE DECOLONIZATION?
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  METROPOLITAN CAUSATION         PERIPHERAL CAUSATION
  ┌───────────────────────┐      ┌───────────────────────┐
  │ Empires became too    │      │ Colonial subjects     │
  │ expensive to maintain │      │ fought for and won    │
  │                       │      │ independence          │
  │ • Post-WWII British   │      │                       │
  │   economic weakness   │      │ • Indian National     │
  │   made empire         │      │   Congress — 50+ years │
  │   unaffordable        │      │   of mobilization     │
  │                       │      │                       │
  │ • Cost-benefit: did   │      │ • Mau Mau, FLN, MPLA, │
  │   empire actually     │      │   FRELIMO — armed     │
  │   pay for post-WWII   │      │   insurgencies        │
  │   Britain?            │      │                       │
  │                       │      │ • Mass nationalist    │
  │ • Gallagher-Robinson: │      │   parties using       │
  │   local collaborative │      │   colonial political  │
  │   structures eroded   │      │   concepts against    │
  │   — formal control    │      │   empire              │
  │   no longer worked    │      │                       │
  └───────────────────────┘      └───────────────────────┘
           │                              │
           └───────────────┬──────────────┘
                           ▼
              SYNTHESIS: Both mattered.
              Without nationalism, no political
              force to demand independence.
              Without metropolitan cost/willingness
              calculus, demands could be suppressed.
              The intersection determined timing.

BRITISH DECOLONIZATION LOGIC
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  PREFERENCE: Negotiate independence before forced out
              → maintain economic/cultural ties through
              Commonwealth → "informal empire" persists

  MECHANISM:
  1. Work with nationalist elites (Nehru, Nkrumah)
  2. Grant internal self-government first
  3. Transfer sovereignty when stable successor clear
  4. Maintain trade, sterling area, military bases

  WORKED: India, Gold Coast/Ghana, Nigeria, Malaya, Kenya
  (eventually, after brutal suppression of Mau Mau)

  FAILED: Palestine (couldn't manage Zionist-Arab conflict,
          handed to UN), Rhodesia (settler minority refused)

INDIA PARTITION — KEY FACTORS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  MOUNTBATTEN SPEED:
  Wavell's plan: 1948 transition — gradual
  Mountbatten's plan: August 1947 — immediately
  Reason: Hindu-Muslim violence already starting,
  faster exit seemed safer
  Result: Violence exploded during partition itself

  RADCLIFFE LINE:
  Cyril Radcliffe: drew borders of Punjab and Bengal
  in 5 weeks — had never been to India before
  Maps were inadequate; census data uncertain
  Announced August 17, two days after independence

  SCALE OF VIOLENCE AND MOVEMENT:
  • 10-20 million people moved (largest forced migration
    in history at the time)
  • 200,000 - 2,000,000 killed (estimates vary enormously)
  • Communal massacres: Muslims leaving India,
    Hindus/Sikhs leaving Pakistan
  • Punjab worst affected; Bengal second

  KASHMIR DISPUTE:
  Maharaja of Kashmir (Hindu ruler, Muslim majority
  population) dithered; Pakistani tribal forces invaded;
  Maharaja acceded to India; First Kashmir War (1947-48)
  → Ceasefire line (now Line of Control) divides Kashmir
  Three more wars follow (1965, 1971, 1999 Kargil)

CONGO CRISIS SEQUENCE
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  June 30, 1960: Independence from Belgium
        │
        ▼ Days later: Army mutiny; Belgian paratroopers return
        │
        ▼ Katanga province secedes (backed by Belgian mining
        │  interests — Union Minière)
        │
        ▼ UN peacekeeping force deployed (ONUC) — largest
        │  to date
        │
        ▼ Patrice Lumumba (PM) requests Soviet aid to
        │  suppress secession; US/Belgium alarmed
        │
        ▼ Mobutu (army colonel) with CIA backing deposes
        │  Lumumba; Lumumba executed (January 1961)
        │
        ▼ Five years of civil war; Katanga reintegrated (1963)
        │
        ▼ Mobutu seizes power (1965); renames country Zaire;
          rules kleptocratically for 32 years

blocks.heading_context: ### Portuguese Model: Metropolitan Collapse Driving Decolonization
blocks.text:
PORTUGUESE DECOLONIZATION — THIRD MODEL
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  METROPOLITAN MILITARY COUP (April 25, 1974)
  Cause: 13 years of colonial warfare in three theaters
         (Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau) — no military path to victory
         — radicalized junior officer corps
         │
         ▼
  Carnation Revolution ends Estado Novo dictatorship
         │
         ▼
  Rapid political negotiation / transfer of power
  Guinea-Bissau: Sept 1974
  Mozambique:    June 1975 (FRELIMO)
  Cape Verde/São Tomé: July 1975
  Angola:        Nov 1975 (immediate civil war — MPLA vs. FNLA vs. UNITA)
         │
         ▼
  Outcome: Most rapid formal decolonization of any European empire
           Angola civil war runs 1975-2002 — Cold War proxy conflict

  CONTRAST WITH OTHER MODELS:
  British: Metropolitan calculation — negotiate before forced out
           → maintain Commonwealth ties → managed continuity
  French:  Metropolitan resistance — fight to hold (Indochina, Algeria)
           → military defeat → forced withdrawal
  Portuguese: Metropolitan state collapse drives decolonization —
              periphery didn't win; metropole imploded

COLD WAR DECOLONIZATION ENTANGLEMENT
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  PATTERN: Both superpowers supported anti-colonial movements
           rhetorically; both tried to install client regimes

  US:                              USSR:
  • Supported European allies'     • Supported liberation movements
    colonial interests when         (ANC, FRELIMO, MPLA, PLO)
    Cold War demanded               materially
  • Iran 1953: CIA overthrows      • Cuba sent troops to Angola (1975)
    Mossadegh (democratically       • Advisors across Africa
    elected, nationalized oil)     • Arms to Egypt (Nasser)
  • Guatemala 1954: CIA
    overthrows Arbenz

  RESULT: Many post-colonial states couldn't be neutral
          → had to choose or manage both superpowers
          → often destabilized by superpower competition

  EXCEPTION: Non-Aligned Movement
  Nehru (India), Nasser (Egypt), Tito (Yugoslavia),
  Sukarno (Indonesia), Nkrumah (Ghana)
  → Bandung Conference (1955) articulates NAM
  → Formal NAM founded 1961 (Belgrade)

blocks.heading_context: ## What Decolonization Did and Didn't Change
blocks.text:
DECOLONIZATION — CHANGE MATRIX
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  CHANGED                          DID NOT CHANGE
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Formal sovereignty transferred   Colonial-era borders preserved
  (flags, currencies, armies)      (arbitrary; split ethnic groups;
                                   created landlocked states)

  Political elite changed          Economic structures often
  (indigenous governing class)     unchanged: extraction economies,
                                   cash crop monocultures

  Colonial law largely             Trade relationships: former
  replaced with national           colonies still traded primarily
  law (but common law              with former metropoles
  systems persist in
  Anglophone Africa)

  Racial hierarchies of            Comprador elite patterns:
  governance formally ended        national bourgeoisie often
                                   integrates into global capital
                                   (Fanon's critique confirmed)

  International legal status:      IMF/World Bank conditionality
  seats in UN, treaty              reproduced structural adjustment
  capacity                         constraints (see dependency theory)

  Psychological/cultural:          Settler land seizures (Zimbabwe,
  post-colonial identity,          South Africa): land tenure not
  literary and cultural            resolved by formal independence
  production
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
